n: In this lecture we will consider histomorphological diagnosis. In forensic medicine, systematic histological examination has gradually found its place over the last two decades, especially in forensic autopsy. Staining with H&E, special stains and immunohistochemistry, that is IHC, help determine the age of an injury, its vitality and the cause of death. Determining the age of an injury helps to reconstruct the scene of the crime and apprehend the suspect, while punishment differs according to the severity of the injury. The plan is as follows: first vitality and age of injury, then morphological and molecular methods, signs of vitality, and after that digital histology, that is WSI.

t: Vitality and age of injury: two questions
n: In violent death the main attention is paid to two questions. The first is vitality: the question of whether the injury was inflicted during life. Here the periods are divided into ante-mortem, agonal and post-mortem. The second is the age of the injury: how long the victim survived after the injury, that is what the survival period was. Remember: vitality and age of injury are not the same. One determines whether the injury was inflicted during life, and the other indicates the time lived.

After an injury, successive changes occur in the organism. First the injury is inflicted, then haemorrhage appears, then infiltration by inflammatory cells is seen, and finally granulation tissue forms. These reactions during life are collectively called vitality. But care is needed: the exit of blood cells from a vessel occurs after death as well. So this sign alone cannot be reliable evidence.

We look at an overview of histological methods. Haematoxylin and eosin, that is H&E, and special stains help assess the age and vitality of an injury. Histology is also used to establish the cause of death and to distinguish natural from unnatural death. H&E shows erythrocytes, inflammation and fibroblasts, but depends on the operator and gives artefacts. Prussian blue and elastic–van Gieson show vital reactions. Immunohistochemistry is based on the antigen–antibody reaction and detects cytokines and inflammatory cells, but there is no single international protocol. Histology alone is not sufficient.

Now we consider the structure of Maiese's review. In the search 632 articles were found, and after removal of duplicates 598 remained. By title and abstract 201 were selected, and in the end 137 scientific articles remained. The articles were divided into three groups: quantitative analysis in biological fluids and tissue, that is 24, immunohistochemistry, that is 84, and RNA studies, that is 20 mRNA and 21 miRNA. The most studied tissue was skin, and the most frequently sought protein was fibronectin, in 15 of 85 articles. There is no standard, internationally recognised method of proving vitality and age of injury. IHC is the most studied and may be regarded as the "gold standard".

t: Case analysis 1: was the injury inflicted during life?
n: The first case analysis. The situation is as follows: on a corpse there are several injuries, and it is assumed that they were inflicted by different persons. Punishment usually differs according to the severity of the injury, so it is necessary to establish the time and order of the injuries. The pathologist puts two questions. Was the injury inflicted during life, in the agonal period or after death? How long did the victim survive after it? Now ask yourself: why is it unreliable to draw conclusions about an injury merely by looking at it?

t: Tissues most often studied in determining the age of injury
n: There are tissues that are studied more often in determining the age of an injury. Skin, skeletal muscle and brain around the injury have been studied most, because in practice they are commonly encountered. In the studies reviewed, mainly incised or crushed injuries were studied. For skin there are more survey studies, for skeletal muscle more experimental studies, and the brain is often met in violent death and there are many studies of injury age as well. The studies relied mainly on animal and autopsy samples, and some were taken from living people.

t: Sample sources: animal, autopsy, living person
n: There are three sources of samples: animal, autopsy and living person. In animals time is controlled, the result is reproducible and the healing process is similar to that of humans, but applicability to humans is uncertain. The autopsy sample is the most realistic and is accurate if the age is known, but documents are insufficient and post-mortem changes, that is putrefactive, interfere. In a sample from a living person, time is recorded precisely, but it is usually taken from sick patients, samples are few, and in a swab there is a risk of a false negative.

We dwell on ethics and sample limitations. Research in humans requires approval from the local ethics committee. The use of living donor tissue is also an important ethical question. Obtaining human samples of known time has ethical problems and is not easy, which is why animal studies are necessary. Attention: a result in animals does not mean a proven result in humans, although markers of high homology may perform a similar function. From a living person, the sample is taken non-invasively, that is a swab. If the volume is insufficient, the result is unreliable, sometimes false negative.

t: Case analysis 2: which sample do we rely on?
n: The second case analysis. Situation: sample A was taken at autopsy, and the time of injury is unknown. Sample B was taken from a living person, and the time is precisely recorded. In A, putrefaction, decomposition, drying, the person's age, the site of the injury and survival time must be taken into account. In B the time is precise, but the sample may be small and a false negative result may occur. Storage in a test tube suppresses the vital reaction. The question is as follows: which sample do you rely on and how do you control the post-mortem effect?

t: Macroscopic assessment: colour of a haematoma
n: In macroscopic assessment, the colour of a haematoma is looked at. Attempts to determine the age of a bruise from its colour have long been used. However, for practical application this method is too variable: the colour of a bruise and the time of its appearance are affected by depth, location and skin colour. Haemorrhage into the soft tissues of the skin may indicate the vitality of a bruise, and change of colour the survival time. Nevertheless, assessing an injury by eye is not a reliable method of proving vitality.

t: H&E, Berlin blue and other stains
n: Now H&E, Berlin blue and other stains. Ordinary histology, that is H&E and Berlin blue, may show changes about 6 hours after injury. Together with H&E, the Prussian blue and elastic–van Gieson stains make vital reactions visible. With H&E, operator and staining artefacts become a problem. The practical use of Berlin blue is limited. In general, histology alone is not sufficient to prove vitality.

Attention: is erythrocyte extravasation reliable? The exit of red blood cells into tissue, that is extravasation, is regarded as a sign of a vital reaction. But extravasation is not proof of vitality. It may appear after death too, so it is not a reliable marker. Resuscitation measures, by maintaining circulation, can cause post-mortem erythrocyte extravasation. In histology there is operator dependence and staining artefacts. Such signs have also been found in skin without vital injury.

The first block of quick questions, basics of histology. Question 1: what is the difference between vitality and age of injury? Answer: vitality means that the injury was formed during life, and age means how long was lived after the injury. Question 2: does H&E alone prove vitality? Answer: no, because it depends on the operator, there are artefacts, and the signs may also occur in skin without vital injury. Question 3: after how many hours from injury can H&E and Berlin blue show a change? Answer: after about 6 hours, but practical use is limited. Remember: erythrocyte extravasation may appear after death too, so it cannot be the sole marker.

About immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence. Immunohistochemistry, IHC, is based on the immunological reaction between antigen and antibody. This reaction makes the desired molecule visible in tissue. The most commonly used stains show cytokines, that is IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, inflammatory cells such as mast cells, and molecules related to injury. The expression of some molecules changes over time, so they can be used to determine the age of injury. IHC and immunofluorescence in early injury show the location of tissue factors. The multiple-staining method makes it possible to detect 3–4 markers at once.

Advantages and disadvantages of IHC. IHC is a morphological method: it shows where molecules are located in injured tissue and how much there is. It is used on paraffin blocks, so old, unsolved cases can be reviewed. Expensive equipment is not required, and the method may be regarded as the gold standard. Disadvantages: there is no single international protocol, and staining quality depends on many factors. Attention: assessment of quantity depends on the operator, so the result may be erroneous or irreproducible.

t: Fibrin and the picro-Mallory stain: timeline
n: Fibrin and the picro-Mallory stain give a timeline. In the picro-Mallory stain, the colour of fibrin changes from red to blue depending on the maturation of the clot. Fibrin is red at 30 minutes–6 hours, violet or blue-violet at 6–12 hours, and blue if older than 24 hours. FXIII regulates cross-linking of fibrin monomers and strengthens the clot. In bone fractures sustained during life, fibrin deposits have been found from 34 minutes to 26 days.

Quantitative markers and electrolytes. The amount of protein is measured by radioimmunoassay, ELISA, electrophoresis, MALDI-TOF, nano-LC MS and HPLC, and ions by atomic absorption spectrophotometry. Magnesium and calcium are important in enzyme regulation and muscle contraction, and zinc increases in the late stage of recovery. Changes in sodium and potassium may be linked to membrane disruption in trauma and to a change in membrane potential. Articles in this direction are few, 24 of 137, and the methods are insufficiently tested for forensic purposes.

t: Case analysis 3: a doubtful IHC result
n: The third case analysis: a doubtful IHC result. Suppose: the corpse is putrefied, and in a skin injury immunohistochemistry for a vital marker gave a positive result. Can the result be trusted? Some authors have shown that IHC is reliable even in a putrefied corpse, but only three such studies were found. Putrefaction disrupts tissue structure. This may affect both the strength of staining and the location of the sign. To reduce error, combined use of morphological and molecular indicators is recommended.

mRNA analysis and real-time PCR. After injury, the level of cytokine and enzyme mRNA changes earlier than protein and histomorphology. The sequence is as follows: injury is inflicted, the mRNA level changes, then the protein level changes and finally the histomorphological change is seen. Real-time PCR, that is polymerase chain reaction, detects even small differences in gene expression. For normalisation a reference gene is needed, since some housekeeping genes are activated after injury.

High-throughput methods and protein analysis. Gene chips, high-throughput sequencing and the 384-well microplate system analyse tens to hundreds of genes at once. Such methods considerably reduce the cost of analysis, make results reproducible and stable, and help in choosing a marker. Western blot and ELISA, that is enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, are more sensitive than immunohistochemistry. A protein microarray analyses many proteins in one sample. Attention: it is hard to compare the results of laboratories, because the procedures are complex and controlling conditions is not easy.

The second block of quick questions, molecular methods. Question: why is mRNA analysis preferable in early injury? Answer: the mRNA level changes earlier than protein and histomorphology. Question: why is a reference gene needed in real-time PCR? Answer: some housekeeping genes rise after injury and normalisation is disrupted. Question: why may microRNA be an early sign? Answer: it regulates protein synthesis, so its change is expected to be seen before the protein. Question: what are the advantage and limitation of measuring electrolytes and proteins? Answer: the result does not depend on the operator, but the method usually works within 48 hours after death.

We compare the time window of the methods. The histological reaction is usually detected after 24 hours, and changes in mRNA and protein in about 12 hours. H&E and Berlin blue show change 6 hours after injury, but practical use is limited. P-selectin, however, was detected in immunohistochemistry 3 minutes after injury, an observation of 1998, an early sign. For early injury mRNA and protein methods suit, and for later injury, histology. Attention: do not rely on one method; morphological and molecular signs are used together.

t: Case analysis 4: a very early injury
n: The fourth case analysis: a very early injury. Situation: the injury was inflicted a few minutes before death. Question: is histology sufficient? No, in the first minutes to hours it cannot decide. The molecular method makes it possible, since mRNA levels change faster than protein and histomorphology. Dressler and colleagues in 1998 observed a strongly positive immunohistochemical reaction to P-selectin 3 minutes after injury. Attention: immediately after death, residual-life phenomena may mimic a vital reaction, so data on the circumstances are also taken into account.

t: Skin and skeletal muscle: stages of healing
n: Stages of healing in skin and skeletal muscle. Healing consists of three stages: inflammation, proliferation and maturation. In the inflammatory stage, in both skin and skeletal muscle, neutrophils and macrophages arrive. In proliferation, re-epithelialisation and granulation tissue form in skin, and in skeletal muscle satellite cells differentiate into myocytes. In forensic medicine, the appearance and disappearance of inflammatory cells is mapped over time. In diabetes, healing differs from ordinary injury, so ordinary parameters may not be suitable.

Biomarkers of brain injury. The central nervous system is very sensitive to mechanical, ischaemic and toxic action. Since neurons are not renewed, brain damage is irreversible. Mechanical injury is often accompanied by epidural, subdural, subarachnoid and parenchymal haemorrhage, and the age of the haemorrhage is assessed by H&E and IHC. Diffuse axonal injury is severe, and early diagnosis is difficult. β-amyloid precursor protein is detected at the site of axonal disruption, which is a sensitive and specific marker. Microglia are activated and reactive astrocytes increase. The dynamics of glial and inflammatory cells are used in determining the time of brain injury.

Post-mortem stability and choice of marker. Putrefaction, decomposition and drying destroy mRNA and proteins, so markers stable after death are chosen. Argininosuccinate lyase mRNA is stable for up to 18 hours, and SNAT2 mRNA for up to 48 hours. The proteins LC3-II and p62 are stable for up to 4 days. The mRNA of matrix metalloproteinase-2 and TIMP-2 was markedly degraded in 12 hours, and cannabinoid receptor-2 mRNA in 3 hours. To eliminate the effect of post-mortem interval, a control group and seasonal factors are taken into account.

Residual-life phenomena and post-mortem manipulations. Death occurs, and after it for a short time cells remain active and may mimic a vital reaction. Ventilation may artificially produce emphysema, and resuscitation haemorrhage. As a result a false vital sign appears, so the circumstances must be checked. As the post-mortem interval lengthens, the reliability of biomarkers falls, whereas immunohistochemistry is relatively resistant.

t: Case analysis 5: a finding after resuscitation
n: The fifth case analysis: a finding after resuscitation. Situation: in the tissue of a corpse that underwent resuscitation, exit of erythrocytes, that is haemorrhage, was found. Because resuscitation maintained circulation, it may produce post-mortem erythrocyte extravasation. Attention: erythrocyte extravasation is not proof of vitality, since it may appear after death too. Question: how will you assess the finding? Compare it with data on the circumstances, the investigation and the medical history.

The third block of quick questions, limitations and errors. Question: what is residual life? Answer: reactions that continue for a short time after death; they may mimic vital ones. Question: what does putrefaction affect? Answer: it lowers the reliability of biomarkers and may alter tissue structure. Question: are normal wound criteria suitable in a person with diabetes? Answer: no, in diabetes wound healing differs. Question: what do resuscitation and ventilation produce? Answer: false signs resembling haemorrhage and emphysema.

The multi-marker approach and analytical models. One indicator is insufficient to determine the age of an injury, whereas combining several indicators reduces error. A model of four mRNAs, up-regulated, unchanged and down-regulated, narrowed the interval of injury age. CD14, CD32B and CD68 together were more specific than a single marker, and in skin injury the interval came out narrower. Probability scoring systems have also been built by scoring morphological features. The mathematical model relies on animal data and calibration against autopsies.

t: Future directions: assessing the age of injury
n: Future directions. Determining the age of an injury at an early stage depends largely on the pathologist's experience. An animal model is needed that takes account of the age and sex of the deceased, cause of death, severity of injury, time after death, season and storage conditions. Combining many markers with high-throughput analysis, and morphology with genomics, proteomics and metabolomics, is anticipated. The mathematical model should rely on large animal studies and be calibrated against human autopsies. In practice, no single multi-marker system has yet been proposed.

Digital WSI and its method of validation. WSI is a high-resolution digital image of an entire glass slide, which is viewed on a computer screen. The requirement of the CAP, that is the College of American Pathologists: at least 60 cases, a two-week washout, concordance must be above 95%. The iForensic design was as follows: 6 forensic pathologists first viewed 100 slides under the microscope, the slides were scanned on an Aperio GT 450 DX, after a two-week washout were assessed on screen in the WSI O3 viewer, and concordance was compared.

Composition of the iForensic slides. One hundred forensically significant glass slides were selected, consisting of various organs and tissues. By manner of death: homicide 10, suicide 15, natural 30, accident 15, medical liability 30. Eighty slides were stained with ordinary haematoxylin and eosin, and 20 with histochemical stains, that is PTAH, PAS, Masson, Perls, Von Kossa, and IHC markers. Scanning took on average 44 seconds, with a file size of 119–997 megabytes, average 640.

iForensic results. Six forensic pathologists, each of whom had performed more than 500 autopsies, assessed 100 slides. Diagnoses by microscope and WSI agreed on average in 97.8%. This is above the CAP threshold, and satisfaction was also high: by CSUQ 6.6 out of 7. File size 119–997 megabytes, average 640. Image quality and ease of navigation on screen were rated highly.

t: Capabilities of WSI: service, research, education
n: The capabilities of WSI show themselves in service, research and education. In service, a high-quality digital image is quickly sent to a specialist elsewhere, consultation takes place in real time, and there is no need to wait for the specimen to be posted. In research, artificial intelligence, that is AI, can quantitatively assess cell density, tissue structure and inflammatory response, which reduces subjectivity. Old cases can also be reviewed; in large and retrospective studies this may give new information. In education, students view the image remotely without being in the laboratory, discuss findings together and receive the opinion of a specialist.

The sixth case analysis: digital consultation. The situation is a teaching example: at autopsy a complex change was found in a preparation of brain tissue. The expert is not fully confident of the diagnosis. The slide is scanned and the digital image is sent to a neuropathologist. He views the image in real time and gives his opinion. Sending a physical specimen usually causes delay, whereas digital exchange removes this delay and speeds up the conclusion. Question: which two advantages does digital consultation give in this case, and which important examination remains obligatory?

t: Conclusion: standard and the complex approach
n: Conclusion. There is as yet no internationally recognised standard method of proving that an injury was inflicted during life and of proving its age. Attention: histology alone is not sufficient proof. A complex approach combining histological, immunohistochemical and genetic methods is necessary. Assessing the age of an injury is complex, so one indicator is not enough, and joint use of several signs reduces error. Digital WSI agreed with the microscope at 97.8%, that is above the 95% threshold. This makes the digital direction promising for the future.
